title: Περὶ ψυχῆς
about: Priam and Hecuba plead in vain. Hector stays at the wall, unyielding as a snake outside its hole, and argues with himself: if he goes in, Polydamas will reproach him; he thinks of laying down his arms and offering Helen and the city’s wealth, then drops the idea, and decides it is better to fight at once and see to whom Zeus gives victory. But when Achilles comes on, shining like fire or the rising sun, trembling takes him and he runs, with Achilles after him like a falcon after a dove. They pass the lookout, the wild fig-tree and the two springs of Scamander, where the Trojan women once washed their clothes, and run three times round the city, in a race with no prize but Hector’s life. On Olympus the gods look on; Zeus pities Hector and asks whether to save him, Athena objects, Zeus gives way, and she goes down from Olympus.

sentences.t:
ὣς τώ γε κλαίοντε προσαυδήτην φίλον υἱὸν
πολλὰ λισσομένω·
sentences.l:
So the two of them, weeping, addressed their dear son,
much beseeching;
sentences.i: So the two of them, weeping, spoke to their dear son, begging him hard;
sentences.n: Priam and Hecuba, who have just pleaded with Hector in turn, go on pleading. τώ γε is the dual ‘those two’, and κλαίοντε and λισσομένω are duals too; προσαυδήτην is the third-person dual imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to, address’. πολλά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘much, greatly’, and λισσομένω is from λίσσομαι ‘beseech’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ Ἕκτορι θυμὸν ἔπειθον,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε μίμν’ Ἀχιλῆα πελώριον ἆσσον ἰόντα.
sentences.l:
nor were they persuading the heart of Hector,
but he kept waiting for huge Achilles, coming closer.
sentences.i: but they did not persuade Hector’s heart; he went on waiting for huge Achilles as he came nearer.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ … ἔπειθον ‘nor were they persuading’: the imperfect of πείθω says they kept trying and kept failing. μίμν’ is μίμνε, the unaugmented imperfect of μίμνω ‘wait for, stay’, with its last vowel elided, and its object is Ἀχιλῆα (one λ, for the metre). πελώριον ‘huge’ is a word for something of awe-inspiring size. ἆσσον is the comparative adverb ‘closer’ and ἰόντα the participle of εἶμι ‘come, go’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ δράκων ἐπὶ χειῇ ὀρέστερος ἄνδρα μένῃσι
βεβρωκὼς κακὰ φάρμακ’,
sentences.l:
And as a serpent of the mountains at its hole waits for a man,
having eaten evil drugs,
sentences.i: And as a mountain serpent waits for a man at its hole, having eaten evil drugs,
sentences.n: A simile begins; ὡς δέ ‘and as’ is answered by ὣς Ἕκτωρ ‘so Hector’ in line 96. δράκων is a serpent, ὀρέστερος is ‘of the mountains’, mountain-dwelling, and χειῇ is a hole or lair. μένῃσι is the subjunctive of μένω ‘wait for’ with the ending -σι, and ἄνδρα is its object. βεβρωκώς is the perfect participle of βιβρώσκω ‘eat’. φάρμακα is ‘drugs’, which can heal or harm; κακά ‘evil’ makes them poisons.

sentences.t:
ἔδυ δέ τέ μιν χόλος αἰνός,
σμερδαλέον δὲ δέδορκεν ἑλισσόμενος περὶ χειῇ·
sentences.l:
and fearsome anger has entered it,
and terribly it glares, curling about its hole;
sentences.i: and a fearsome anger has entered it, and it glares terribly, curling about its hole;
sentences.n: The simile goes on. ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘enter, sink into’, with μιν ‘it’ as object and χόλος αἰνός ‘fearsome anger’ as subject; δέ τέ has the general τε of similes. σμερδαλέον is an adverb, ‘terribly’. δέδορκεν is the perfect of δέρκομαι ‘look’ with a present sense, ‘glares’, and ἑλισσόμενος is the participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn, coil’, here ‘curling about’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἄσβεστον ἔχων μένος οὐχ ὑπεχώρει
πύργῳ ἔπι προὔχοντι φαεινὴν ἀσπίδ’ ἐρείσας·
sentences.l:
so Hector, having unquenchable might, did not give way,
his shining shield propped against the jutting tower;
sentences.i: so Hector, with his might unquenched, did not give way, his shining shield propped against a jutting tower;
sentences.n: The comparison closes: ὣς Ἕκτωρ ‘so Hector’ answers ὡς δέ in line 93. ἄσβεστον ‘unquenchable’ goes with μένος ‘might’, and ὑπεχώρει is the imperfect of ὑποχωρέω ‘give way, retreat’. προὔχοντι is the contracted form of προέχοντι, ‘jutting out’, with πύργῳ ‘tower’; πύργῳ ἔπι is ‘against the tower’. ἐρείσας is the aorist participle of ἐρείδω ‘prop, lean’, with φαεινὴν ἀσπίδ’ ‘shining shield’ as its object.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: Hector now argues with himself; his speech starts in the next unit. The line is a formula, the same as the one that introduces Odysseus’ debate with himself at 11.403. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, troubled’, and εἶπε the aorist of εἶπον ‘say’. πρὸς ὃν … θυμόν is ‘to his own heart’: ὅν is the possessive ‘his own’, and μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’ goes with θυμόν.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι ἐγών, εἰ μέν κε πύλας καὶ τείχεα δύω,
Πουλυδάμας μοι πρῶτος ἐλεγχείην ἀναθήσει,
sentences.l:
“Oh me, if I go in through the gates and the walls,
Polydamas will be the first to lay disgrace upon me,
sentences.i: “Oh me! If I go in through the gates and the walls, Polydamas will be the first to lay disgrace upon me,
sentences.n: Hector’s speech to himself begins, and it runs to line 130. ὤ μοι ἐγών is ‘oh me’. The condition εἰ μέν κε … δύω is εἰ with κε and the aorist subjunctive of δύω ‘go in, enter’; its μέν is answered by εἰ δέ κεν at line 111. Πουλυδάμας is Polydamas, with the epic spelling πουλυ- for πολυ-. ἐλεγχείην is the accusative of ἐλεγχείη ‘reproach, disgrace’, and ἀναθήσει the future of ἀνατίθημι ‘put upon, lay on’, with μοι ‘on me’.

sentences.t:
ὅς μ’ ἐκέλευε Τρωσὶ ποτὶ πτόλιν ἡγήσασθαι
νύχθ’ ὕπο τήνδ’ ὀλοὴν ὅτε τ’ ὤρετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l:
who ordered me to lead the Trojans to the city
during this baneful night, when heavenly Achilles rose.
sentences.i: he who told me to lead the Trojans to the city during this baneful night, when heavenly Achilles rose up.
sentences.n: ὅς refers to Polydamas, and the clause recalls his advice. ἐκέλευε is the imperfect of κελεύω ‘order, urge’, followed by ἡγήσασθαι ‘to lead’ (aorist infinitive middle), with Τρωσί ‘the Trojans’ and ποτὶ πτόλιν (= πρὸς πόλιν) ‘to the city’. νύχθ’ ὕπο τήνδ’ ὀλοήν is ‘under this baneful night’, that is, during it: νύχθ’ is νύκτα with the vowel elided, and ὕπο stands after its noun. ὤρετο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, so ‘rose’. The Greek does not say which night is meant.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην· ἦ τ’ ἂν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν.
sentences.l: But I did not obey; truly much better it would have been.
sentences.i: But I did not obey — and it would surely have been far better if I had.
sentences.n: πιθόμην is the aorist middle of πείθομαι ‘obey’. ἦ τ’ ἂν … ἦεν is ‘truly it would have been’, ἦεν being ἦν with the epic ending, and κέρδιον is the comparative ‘better, more profitable’ with πολύ ‘much’. The first half of the line is a statement of fact, the second a regret: it would have been better if he had obeyed.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ ὤλεσα λαὸν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἐμῇσιν,
αἰδέομαι Τρῶας καὶ Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους,
sentences.l:
But now, since I destroyed the people by my own wanton-follies,
I feel shame before the Trojans and the Trojan women trailing-robed,
sentences.i: But now, since I destroyed the army through my own wanton folly, I am ashamed before the Trojans and the Trojan women with their trailing robes,
sentences.n: Hector gives his reason: νῦν δ’ ἐπεί ‘but now, since’. ὤλεσα is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’ and λαόν ‘the people, the army’. ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἐμῇσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘by my own wanton follies’. αἰδέομαι ‘I feel shame before’ takes the accusatives Τρῶας and Τρῳάδας ‘Trojan women’, and ἑλκεσιπέπλους ‘trailing-robed’ is ἕλκω ‘drag’ + πέπλος ‘robe’. Line 105 is word for word the line Hector speaks to Andromache at 6.442.

sentences.t: μή ποτέ τις εἴπῃσι κακώτερος ἄλλος ἐμεῖο·
sentences.l: lest at some time some other, a baser man than I, should say:
sentences.i: lest some other man, baser than I, ever say:
sentences.n: μή ποτέ … εἴπῃσι ‘lest ever … say’ is a clause of fear introduced by μή, with the aorist subjunctive of εἶπον in the -σι form. κακώτερος is the comparative of κακός ‘base’, and ἐμεῖο is ἐμοῦ, the genitive of comparison, ‘than I’. What he fears they will say comes in the next unit.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ ἧφι βίηφι πιθήσας ὤλεσε λαόν.
sentences.l: ‘Hector, obeying his own might, destroyed the people.’
sentences.i: ‘Hector, trusting in his own might, destroyed the army.’
sentences.n: These are the words Hector imagines, in inner quotation marks. ἧφι βίηφι is ‘his own might’, with the old instrumental ending -φι on both words, doing the work of a dative after πιθήσας. πιθήσας is the aorist participle of πιθέω, the epic form of πείθομαι ‘obey, yield to’, so the Greek says Hector obeyed his own strength; the English second layer gives the sense, trusting in it. ὤλεσε is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’ and answers ὤλεσα in line 104.
sentences.mark: A Trojan speaks, as Hector imagines it

sentences.t: ὣς ἐρέουσιν·
sentences.l: So they will say;
sentences.i: That is what they will say;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐρέουσιν ‘so they will say’: ἐρέουσιν is the future of εἶπον in its epic form, third person plural. The unit ends at the ano teleia, and Hector turns to what he would rather do.

sentences.t:
ἐμοὶ δὲ τότ’ ἂν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη
ἄντην ἢ Ἀχιλῆα κατακτείναντα νέεσθαι,
ἠέ κεν αὐτῷ ὀλέσθαι ἐϋκλειῶς πρὸ πόληος.
sentences.l:
but for me then much better it would be
face to face either, having killed Achilles, to go home,
or myself to perish at his hands with fair fame before the city.
sentences.i: But then it would be much better for me to meet him face to face and either kill Achilles and go home, or perish at his hands with fair renown before the city.
sentences.n: ἐμοὶ δὲ τότ’ ἂν … εἴη is the optative with ἂν, ‘for me then it would be’, with κέρδιον ‘better’ and πολύ ‘much’. ἄντην means ‘face to face’. The two choices are ἢ … νέεσθαι and ἠέ … ὀλέσθαι ‘either … to return’ and ‘or … to perish’: Ἀχιλῆα κατακτείναντα is the accusative with the aorist participle ‘having killed Achilles’, and αὐτῷ ‘him’ (Achilles, in the dative) goes with ὀλέσθαι, the aorist infinitive of ὄλλυμαι, ‘perish at his hands’. ἐϋκλειῶς is an adverb, ἐϋ- ‘well’ + κλέος ‘fame’; πόληος is the epic genitive of πόλις.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν ἀσπίδα μὲν καταθείομαι ὀμφαλόεσσαν
καὶ κόρυθα βριαρήν,
sentences.l:
But if I should lay down my bossed shield
and my weighty helmet,
sentences.i: But if I were to lay down my bossed shield and my heavy helmet,
sentences.n: A second plan: εἰ δέ κεν ‘but if’ is the other side of εἰ μέν κε in line 99. καταθείομαι is the aorist subjunctive middle of κατατίθημι ‘put down’, in the epic form -θείομαι. ὀμφαλόεσσαν ‘bossed’ comes from ὀμφαλός ‘navel, boss’, the raised centre of a shield, and βριαρήν ‘weighty, heavy’ belongs to κόρυθα ‘helmet’.

sentences.t:
δόρυ δὲ πρὸς τεῖχος ἐρείσας
αὐτὸς ἰὼν Ἀχιλῆος ἀμύμονος ἀντίος ἔλθω
καί οἱ ὑπόσχωμαι Ἑλένην καὶ κτήμαθ’ ἅμ’ αὐτῇ,
sentences.l:
and, propping my spear against the wall,
myself going should come face to face with blameless Achilles
and promise him Helen and the possessions together with her,
sentences.i: and, propping my spear against the wall, were to go myself to meet blameless Achilles and promise him Helen and the possessions along with her,
sentences.n: The condition goes on with ἐρείσας ‘propping’ (aorist participle) and two aorist subjunctives, ἔλθω ‘come’ and ὑπόσχωμαι ‘promise’. ἀντίος ἔλθω takes the genitive Ἀχιλῆος, ‘come to meet’. ἀμύμονος is the stock epithet, ‘blameless’; the real sense of the word is not known. Ἑλένην and κτήμαθ’ (κτήματα ‘possessions’) are what he would promise, and οἱ is ‘to him’.

sentences.t:
πάντα μάλ’ ὅσσά τ’ Ἀλέξανδρος κοίλῃς ἐνὶ νηυσὶν
ἠγάγετο Τροίηνδ’, ἥ τ’ ἔπλετο νείκεος ἀρχή,
sentences.l:
all of it, as much as Alexander in his hollow ships
brought to Troy, she who was the beginning of the quarrel,
sentences.i: all of it, as much as Alexander brought to Troy in his hollow ships, she who was the beginning of the quarrel,
sentences.n: πάντα μάλ’ ὅσσα ‘all, as many as’ sums up the possessions. Ἀλέξανδρος is Paris. ἠγάγετο is the aorist middle of ἄγω, ‘brought (for himself)’, and Τροίηνδ’ is ‘to Troy’, the ending -δε meaning ‘toward’. ἥ is feminine, so it refers to Helen and not to the goods. ἔπλετο is the aorist of πέλομαι ‘come to be’, and νείκεος is the genitive of νεῖκος ‘quarrel’.

sentences.t:
δωσέμεν Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν ἄγειν, ἅμα δ’ ἀμφὶς Ἀχαιοῖς
ἄλλ’ ἀποδάσσεσθαι ὅσα τε πτόλις ἥδε κέκευθε·
sentences.l:
to give to the sons of Atreus to lead away, and at the same time, apart, to the Achaeans
to share out other things, as many as this city has hidden away;
sentences.i: to give to the sons of Atreus to take away, and at the same time, separately, to the Achaeans to share out the other things, all that this city keeps hidden away;
sentences.n: The promise continues. δωσέμεν is the epic future infinitive of δίδωμι ‘give’, with Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν ‘to the sons of Atreus’ (Agamemnon and Menelaus) and ἄγειν ‘to lead away’. ἅμα δ’ ἀμφίς is ‘and at the same time, apart’, with Ἀχαιοῖς ‘to the Achaeans’; ἀποδάσσεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἀποδατέομαι ‘divide off among themselves’, with ἄλλ’ (ἄλλα) ‘other things’ as its object. ὅσα τε … κέκευθε is ‘as many as … has hidden’, the perfect of κεύθω ‘hide’, and πτόλις is πόλις.

sentences.t:
Τρωσὶν δ’ αὖ μετόπισθε γερούσιον ὅρκον ἕλωμαι
μή τι κατακρύψειν, ἀλλ’ ἄνδιχα πάντα δάσασθαι
κτῆσιν ὅσην πτολίεθρον ἐπήρατον ἐντὸς ἐέργει·
sentences.i: and afterwards, in turn, take from the Trojans an elders’ oath that they will hide nothing, but divide everything into two shares, all the property that the lovely citadel holds shut within;
sentences.n: The third part of the offer is an oath. Τρωσὶν δ’ αὖ μετόπισθε is ‘and for the Trojans, in turn, afterwards’; γερούσιον ὅρκον is ‘an elders’ oath’, an oath of the council of elders, and ἕλωμαι is the aorist subjunctive middle of αἱρέω ‘take’. The dative Τρωσίν is loose, but the sense is that the Trojans are made to swear. The oath itself is in the infinitives μή τι κατακρύψειν ‘not to hide anything’ (future) and ἄνδιχα … δάσασθαι ‘to divide in two’ (aorist of δατέομαι). κτῆσιν ‘property’ is the object of δάσασθαι, with ὅσην ‘as much as’; πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’ is the subject of ἐντὸς ἐέργει ‘holds shut within’, and ἐπήρατον means ‘lovely’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός;
sentences.l: But why indeed has my dear heart talked these things over with me?
sentences.i: But why has my own heart talked all this over with me?
sentences.n: Hector breaks off his imagined bargain. The line is also Odysseus’ question to himself at 11.407. τί ‘why’ is followed by the particle ἤ, ‘indeed’; ταῦτα is ‘these things’, μοι ‘with me’, and διελέξατο is the aorist middle of διαλέγομαι ‘talk over’. φίλος θυμός is ‘my dear heart’, the same θυμός he addressed in line 98.

sentences.t:
μή μιν ἐγὼ μὲν ἵκωμαι ἰών, ὃ δέ μ’ οὐκ ἐλεήσει
οὐδέ τί μ’ αἰδέσεται,
sentences.l:
Lest I, for my part, go and come to him, and he will not pity me
nor at all respect me,
sentences.i: for fear that I go up to him and he will neither pity me nor show me any respect,
sentences.n: μή … ἵκωμαι is a clause of fear: ἵκωμαι is the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’, with μιν ‘him’, and ἰών ‘going’. The μέν after ἐγώ is answered by ὃ δέ ‘but he’. ἐλεήσει ‘will pity’ and αἰδέσεται ‘will respect’ are futures, which a fear clause allows. οὐκ … οὐδέ τι is ‘not … nor at all’.

sentences.t:
κτενέει δέ με γυμνὸν ἐόντα
αὔτως ὥς τε γυναῖκα, ἐπεί κ’ ἀπὸ τεύχεα δύω.
sentences.l:
but will kill me, being naked,
just so, like a woman, when I have put off my armour.
sentences.i: but will kill me defenceless, just as he would a woman, once I have put off my armour.
sentences.n: κτενέει is the future of κτείνω ‘kill’. γυμνὸν ἐόντα is ‘being naked’, and here ‘naked’ means stripped of armour. αὔτως ὥς τε γυναῖκα ‘just so, like a woman’ means helpless, unable to fight back. ἐπεί κ’ ἀπὸ τεύχεα δύω is ‘when I have put off my armour’: ἀπὸ … δύω is ἀποδύω, ‘strip off’, split by tmesis and in the aorist subjunctive, and τεύχεα is ‘armour’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν πως νῦν ἔστιν ἀπὸ δρυὸς οὐδ’ ἀπὸ πέτρης
τῷ ὀαριζέμεναι,
sentences.l:
In no way is it now possible, from oak or from rock,
to converse with him,
sentences.i: There is no way now to talk with him from an oak or from a rock,
sentences.n: οὐ μέν πως … ἔστιν is ‘there is in no way’, with νῦν ‘now’. ἀπὸ δρυὸς οὐδ’ ἀπὸ πέτρης ‘from oak or from rock’ is a proverbial phrase whose exact sense is not known; Hector’s point is that this is no time for gentle talk. ὀαριζέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ὀαρίζω ‘talk familiarly, converse’, and τῷ ‘with him’ is the article used as a pronoun.

sentences.t:
ἅ τε παρθένος ἠΐθεός τε
παρθένος ἠΐθεός τ’ ὀαρίζετον ἀλλήλοιιν.
sentences.l:
such talk as a maiden and a young man,
a maiden and a young man, converse with one another.
sentences.i: such talk as a maiden and a young man, a maiden and a young man, hold with one another.
sentences.n: ὀαρίζετον is the dual of ὀαρίζω, and ἀλλήλοιιν is the dual ‘each other’, so the pair is the maiden and the young man (ἠΐθεος). ἅ is a neuter plural used as an inner object, ‘such things as they talk’, and ἅ τε has the general τε. The words παρθένος ἠΐθεός τε are said twice.

sentences.t: βέλτερον αὖτ’ ἔριδι ξυνελαυνέμεν ὅττι τάχιστα·
sentences.l: Better, on the contrary, to drive together in strife as quickly as possible;
sentences.i: It is better, rather, to join in strife at once, as quickly as can be;
sentences.n: βέλτερον is the comparative ‘better’; αὖτ’ is αὖτε, ‘on the other hand’. ἔριδι ξυνελαυνέμεν is ‘to drive together in strife’, that is, to meet in fight: ξυν- is the old spelling of συν-, and -έμεν is the epic infinitive ending. ὅττι τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’.

sentences.t: εἴδομεν ὁπποτέρῳ κεν Ὀλύμπιος εὖχος ὀρέξῃ.
sentences.l: let us see to which of the two the Olympian will stretch out the boast.”
sentences.i: let us see to which of us two the Olympian will grant the triumph.”
sentences.n: εἴδομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of οἶδα (= εἰδῶμεν), ‘let us see, find out’. ὁπποτέρῳ is ‘to which of two’. Ὀλύμπιος alone is Zeus, not named. ὀρέξῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out, hold out’, and εὖχος is ‘boast’, the glory of winning. This closes Hector’s speech to himself.

sentences.t: ὣς ὅρμαινε μένων,
sentences.l: So he pondered, waiting,
sentences.i: So he pondered, standing there,
sentences.n: ὣς ὅρμαινε closes Hector’s debate. ὅρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘turn over in the mind, ponder’, and μένων the present participle of μένω ‘stay, wait’. In the next unit Achilles reaches him.

sentences.t:
ὃ δέ οἱ σχεδὸν ἦλθεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἶσος Ἐνυαλίῳ κορυθάϊκι πτολεμιστῇ
σείων Πηλιάδα μελίην κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον
δεινήν·
sentences.l:
but near him came Achilles,
equal to Enyalius, the helmet-shaking warrior,
shaking the Pelian ash-spear over his right shoulder,
terrible;
sentences.i: but Achilles came near him, like Enyalius the helmet-shaking warrior, shaking his terrible Pelian ash-spear over his right shoulder;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ is Achilles, named at the end of the line, and οἱ ‘to him’ goes with σχεδόν ‘near’. ἶσος ‘equal to’ takes Ἐνυαλίῳ, the dative of Enyalius, a name of the war-god. κορυθάϊκι is the dative of κορυθάϊξ, ‘helmet-shaking’, from κόρυς ‘helmet’ and a form of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, shake’; the formation and exact sense are not certain. πτολεμιστῇ is ‘warrior’ (πτόλεμος is the epic form of πόλεμος ‘war’). σείων is ‘shaking’, Πηλιάδα ‘Pelian’, μελίην ‘ash-spear’, and δεινήν ‘terrible’ agrees with μελίην; κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον is ‘over his right shoulder’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ χαλκὸς ἐλάμπετο εἴκελος αὐγῇ
ἢ πυρὸς αἰθομένου ἢ ἠελίου ἀνιόντος.
sentences.l:
and around him the bronze shone, like the glare
either of burning fire or of the rising sun.
sentences.i: and the bronze about him shone like the glare either of blazing fire or of the rising sun.
sentences.n: ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’, and ἐλάμπετο the imperfect middle of λάμπω ‘shine’. εἴκελος ‘like’ takes the dative αὐγῇ ‘glare’; the genitives πυρὸς αἰθομένου (‘burning fire’) and ἠελίου ἀνιόντος (‘the sun rising’) depend on αὐγῇ, with ἢ … ἢ ‘either … or’.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορα δ’, ὡς ἐνόησεν, ἕλε τρόμος·
sentences.l: And Hector, when he perceived him, trembling seized;
sentences.i: And when Hector saw him, a trembling took hold of him;
sentences.n: Ἕκτορα is the object of ἕλε, the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω ‘seize’, and τρόμος ‘trembling’ is the subject. ὡς ἐνόησεν is ‘when he noticed’, ἐνόησεν being the aorist of νοέω.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἔτλη
αὖθι μένειν, ὀπίσω δὲ πύλας λίπε, βῆ δὲ φοβηθείς·
sentences.l:
and he no longer brought himself
to stay there, but left the gates behind and went, frightened;
sentences.i: and he could no longer bring himself to stay where he was, but left the gates behind him and set off in fear;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἔτλη is ‘and then no longer did he bring himself’, ἔτλη being the aorist of τλάω ‘endure, bring oneself to’, with μένειν ‘to stay’ and αὖθι ‘right there’. λίπε is the unaugmented aorist of λείπω ‘leave’, and ὀπίσω ‘behind’ goes with it. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’. φοβηθείς is the aorist passive participle of φοβέομαι ‘be frightened’; the verb also means ‘flee’, which is what follows.

sentences.t: Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἐπόρουσε ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι πεποιθώς.
sentences.l: but the son of Peleus sprang on, trusting in his rushing feet.
sentences.i: and the son of Peleus sprang forward, trusting in his rushing feet.
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Peleus’, Achilles. ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘spring at, rush on’. πεποιθώς is the perfect participle of πείθω, used with a present sense, ‘trusting’, and takes the dative ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι ‘on his rushing feet’ (κραιπνός ‘rushing’).

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε κίρκος ὄρεσφιν ἐλαφρότατος πετεηνῶν
ῥηϊδίως οἴμησε μετὰ τρήρωνα πέλειαν,
sentences.l:
As a falcon in the mountains, lightest of winged things,
easily darted after a timorous dove,
sentences.i: As a falcon in the mountains, the lightest of winged things, darts easily after a timorous dove,
sentences.n: A simile; ἠΰτε ‘like as’ introduces it. κίρκος is a falcon, and ὄρεσφιν ‘in the mountains’ has the old ending -φιν. ἐλαφρότατος πετεηνῶν is the superlative ‘lightest’ with the genitive ‘of winged things’. οἴμησε is the aorist of οἰμάω ‘dart, swoop’; as in similes generally, the aorist states what happens in a typical case. μετά with the accusative is ‘after’. τρήρωνα is the adjective ‘timorous’, from τρέω ‘tremble’, and goes with πέλειαν ‘dove’.

sentences.t: ἣ δέ θ’ ὕπαιθα φοβεῖται,
sentences.l: and she from beneath flees in fear,
sentences.i: and she flees in fear from underneath him,
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and she’ is the dove, and θ’ is the general τε of similes. φοβεῖται is the present of φοβέομαι ‘take fright, flee’. ὕπαιθα is an adverb meaning ‘from beneath’ or ‘to one side’; which picture the poet has in mind, the dove slipping out from under the falcon or swerving aside, is not certain.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐγγύθεν ὀξὺ λεληκὼς
ταρφέ’ ἐπαΐσσει, ἑλέειν τέ ἑ θυμὸς ἀνώγει·
sentences.l:
and he, from close by, having screamed shrilly,
often darts at her, and his heart bids him seize her;
sentences.i: while he, close behind, screaming shrilly, darts at her again and again, and his heart bids him catch her;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is the falcon. ἐγγύθεν is ‘from near’. λεληκώς is the perfect participle of λάσκω ‘cry out’, with a present sense, and ὀξύ ‘shrilly’ is used as an adverb. ταρφέ’ is ταρφέα, a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘often, again and again’. ἐπαΐσσει is ‘darts at’. ἑλέειν is the aorist infinitive of αἱρέω ‘seize’, ἑ ‘her’, and ἀνώγει ‘bids’, from ἄνωγα.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἐμμεμαὼς ἰθὺς πέτετο, τρέσε δ’ Ἕκτωρ
τεῖχος ὕπο Τρώων, λαιψηρὰ δὲ γούνατ’ ἐνώμα.
sentences.l:
so he flew straight on, eager, and Hector took fright
beneath the wall of the Trojans, and set his quick knees moving.
sentences.i: So Achilles flew straight on, eager, and Hector fled in terror under the wall of the Trojans, setting his quick knees moving.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ‘so, then, he’ finishes the simile; the subject is Achilles. ἐμμεμαώς is the perfect participle ‘eager’, ἰθύς ‘straight on’, and πέτετο the imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’. τρέσε is the aorist of τρέω ‘tremble, flee in fear’. τεῖχος ὕπο Τρώων is ‘under the wall of the Trojans’, with ὕπο after its noun. λαιψηρά is ‘quick’, γούνατ’ is γούνατα ‘knees’, and ἐνώμα the imperfect of νωμάω ‘ply, set moving’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ παρὰ σκοπιὴν καὶ ἐρινεὸν ἠνεμόεντα
τείχεος αἰὲν ὑπ’ ἐκ κατ’ ἀμαξιτὸν ἐσσεύοντο,
sentences.l:
And they, past the lookout and the windy wild fig-tree,
ever from under the wall, along the wagon-road, were hurrying,
sentences.i: And they hurried on along the wagon-road, past the lookout and the windy wild fig-tree, always out from under the wall,
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are Hector and Achilles; the verb is plural, not dual. σκοπιή is a lookout and ἐρινεός a wild fig-tree, with ἠνεμόεντα ‘windy’ (ἄνεμος ‘wind’) agreeing with it; παρά with the accusative is ‘past’. τείχεος αἰὲν ὑπ’ ἐκ is ‘ever out from under the wall’: ὑπ’ ἐκ is ὑπέκ with the genitive, and αἰέν is ‘always’. How exactly the phrase pictures their course is not certain. κατ’ ἀμαξιτόν is ‘along the wagon-road’, and ἐσσεύοντο the imperfect of σεύομαι ‘hurry’, with doubled σ for the metre.

sentences.t: κρουνὼ δ’ ἵκανον καλλιρρόω·
sentences.l: and they reached the two springs, fair-flowing;
sentences.i: and they reached the two fair-flowing springs;
sentences.n: κρουνώ and καλλιρρόω are duals in the accusative, ‘the two springs’ and ‘fair-flowing’ (καλλίρροος). ἵκανον is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘reach’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ πηγαὶ
δοιαὶ ἀναΐσσουσι Σκαμάνδρου δινήεντος.
sentences.l:
and there springs,
two, spring up of eddying Scamander.
sentences.i: and there the two springs of eddying Scamander spring up.
sentences.n: ἔνθα δέ ‘and there’; πηγαί ‘springs’ with δοιαί ‘two’ is the subject of ἀναΐσσουσι, ‘spring up’. Σκαμάνδρου δινήεντος is ‘of eddying Scamander’, the river by Troy; δινήεις is ‘eddying’ (δίνη ‘eddy’).

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν γάρ θ’ ὕδατι λιαρῷ ῥέει, ἀμφὶ δὲ καπνὸς
γίγνεται ἐξ αὐτῆς ὡς εἰ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο·
sentences.l:
For the one flows with warm water, and around it smoke
arises from it, as if from a burning fire;
sentences.i: For one of them flows with warm water, and smoke rises around it from the spring, as if from a burning fire;
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν γάρ θ’ ‘for the one’ is one of the two springs, and its μέν is answered by ἣ δ’ ἑτέρη in the next unit. λιαρῷ is ‘warm’. ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’. καπνός means ‘smoke’; here it is the steam of the hot water. ὡς εἰ is ‘as if’, with πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο ‘from burning fire’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἑτέρη θέρεϊ προρέει ἐϊκυῖα χαλάζῃ,
ἢ χιόνι ψυχρῇ ἢ ἐξ ὕδατος κρυστάλλῳ.
sentences.l:
but the other flows forth in summer like hail,
or cold snow, or ice from water.
sentences.i: but the other flows forth in summer like hail, or cold snow, or ice made from water.
sentences.n: ἑτέρη is ‘the other’. θέρεϊ is the dative of θέρος ‘summer’, and προρέει is ‘flows forth’. ἐϊκυῖα, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, is ‘like’ and takes the datives χαλάζῃ ‘hail’, χιόνι ψυχρῇ ‘cold snow’ and κρυστάλλῳ ‘ice’; ἐξ ὕδατος is ‘out of water’. The likeness is in the water’s coldness.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτάων πλυνοὶ εὐρέες ἐγγὺς ἔασι
καλοὶ λαΐνεοι,
sentences.l:
And there, beside them, wide washing-places are near,
fair, of stone,
sentences.i: And there, close beside them, are wide washing-places, fair ones, made of stone,
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτάων is ‘and there beside them’: αὐτάων is the epic genitive plural, and ἐπί with the genitive means ‘near’. πλυνοί are washing-places, basins where clothes were washed; the Odyssey has the same word. εὐρέες is ‘wide’, ἐγγύς ‘near’, ἔασι the epic form of εἰσί ‘are’, καλοί ‘fair’ and λαΐνεοι ‘of stone’.

sentences.t:
ὅθι εἵματα σιγαλόεντα
πλύνεσκον Τρώων ἄλοχοι καλαί τε θύγατρες
τὸ πρὶν ἐπ’ εἰρήνης πρὶν ἐλθεῖν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
where glossy garments
the wives of the Trojans and their fair daughters used to wash
formerly in peace, before there came the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: where the wives of the Trojans and their fair daughters used to wash their glossy garments in former days in peace, before the sons of the Achaeans came.
sentences.n: ὅθι is ‘where’. εἵματα σιγαλόεντα are ‘glossy garments’. πλύνεσκον is the iterative imperfect of πλύνω ‘wash’, with -σκον for ‘used to’; ἄλοχοι are ‘wives’ and θύγατρες ‘daughters’. τὸ πρίν ‘formerly’ and ἐπ’ εἰρήνης ‘in peace’ are followed by πρὶν ἐλθεῖν, ‘before … came’, with the infinitive after πρίν. Line 156 is word for word a line Achilles speaks at 9.403.

sentences.t: τῇ ῥα παραδραμέτην φεύγων ὃ δ’ ὄπισθε διώκων·
sentences.l: By this way the two ran past, the one fleeing, the other behind pursuing;
sentences.i: By this way the two of them ran past, one in flight and the other behind him in pursuit;
sentences.n: τῇ ῥα is ‘by that way, then’. παραδραμέτην is the dual aorist of παρατρέχω ‘run past’. φεύγων and διώκων are the participles of φεύγω ‘flee’ and διώκω ‘pursue’, and ὃ δ’ ὄπισθε is ‘and the other behind’.

sentences.t:
πρόσθε μὲν ἐσθλὸς ἔφευγε, δίωκε δέ μιν μέγ’ ἀμείνων
καρπαλίμως,
sentences.l:
In front a good man fled, but pursuing him was one far better
swiftly,
sentences.i: In front a good man was fleeing, but one far better was pursuing him, swiftly,
sentences.n: πρόσθε is ‘in front’. ἐσθλός ‘good’ is said of Hector, and μέγ’ ἀμείνων ‘far better’ of Achilles (ἀμείνων is the comparative of ἀγαθός); the clause means that the pursuer is much the stronger. δίωκε is the unaugmented imperfect of διώκω, with μιν ‘him’. καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐχ ἱερήϊον οὐδὲ βοείην
ἀρνύσθην, ἅ τε ποσσὶν ἀέθλια γίγνεται ἀνδρῶν,
sentences.l:
since not a sacrificial animal nor an oxhide
were the two striving to win, which become contest-prizes for the feet of men,
sentences.i: since the two were not striving to win a sacrificial animal or an oxhide, the sort of prizes in contests that men’s feet run for,
sentences.n: ἐπεί gives the reason. ἱερήϊον is an animal for sacrifice and βοείην an oxhide (a feminine adjective used as a noun). ἀρνύσθην is the dual imperfect of ἄρνυμαι ‘strive to win’. ἅ τε ‘such as’ introduces the usual prizes: ἀέθλια ‘contest-prizes’ with ποσσίν ‘for the feet’ (epic dative plural) and ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’, that is, prizes of foot-races.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ περὶ ψυχῆς θέον Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο.
sentences.l: but they were running for the life of Hector, tamer of horses.
sentences.i: but they were running for the life of Hector, tamer of horses.
sentences.n: ἀλλά sets the true stake against the prizes just named. περὶ ψυχῆς is ‘for the life’, with περί and the genitive ‘for the sake of’; ψυχή is ‘life’ here. θέον is the imperfect of θέω ‘run’, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘tamer of horses’, genitive, agrees with Ἕκτορος.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀεθλοφόροι περὶ τέρματα μώνυχες ἵπποι
ῥίμφα μάλα τρωχῶσι·
sentences.l:
And as when prize-bearing solid-hoofed horses around the turning-posts
very nimbly run;
sentences.i: And as when prize-bearing, solid-hoofed horses run very nimbly around the turning-posts;
sentences.n: A second simile, for the speed of the race. ἀεθλοφόροι is ‘prize-bearing’ (ἆθλον ‘prize’ + φέρω ‘bear’) and μώνυχες ‘solid-hoofed’. τέρματα are the turning-posts (τέρμα is ‘end, limit’), the marks the horses round. ῥίμφα is ‘nimbly’, and τρωχῶσι the subjunctive of τρωχάω ‘run’, after ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ μέγα κεῖται ἄεθλον
ἢ τρίπος ἠὲ γυνὴ ἀνδρὸς κατατεθνηῶτος·
sentences.l:
and the great prize lies there,
either a tripod or a woman, of a man who has died;
sentences.i: and a great prize lies set out, either a tripod or a woman, for a man who has died;
sentences.n: τὸ δὲ μέγα κεῖται ἄεθλον is ‘and the great prize lies there’; here ἄεθλον means the prize, not the contest. ἢ τρίπος ἠὲ γυνή is ‘either a tripod or a woman’. ἀνδρὸς κατατεθνηῶτος is the genitive of a perfect participle of καταθνήσκω, ‘of a man who has died’; the prizes are those offered for a dead man, as at funeral games.

sentences.t:
ὣς τὼ τρὶς Πριάμοιο πόλιν πέρι δινηθήτην
καρπαλίμοισι πόδεσσι·
sentences.l:
so the two three times around the city of Priam whirled
on quick feet;
sentences.i: So the two of them circled the city of Priam three times on quick feet;
sentences.n: ὣς τώ ‘so the two’ finishes the simile. δινηθήτην is the dual aorist passive of δινέω ‘whirl, wheel round’, so ‘whirled round’. τρίς is ‘three times’, and πόλιν πέρι is περὶ πόλιν with the preposition after its noun. καρπαλίμοισι πόδεσσι is ‘on quick feet’, the dative plural in -εσσι.

sentences.t: θεοὶ δ’ ἐς πάντες ὁρῶντο·
sentences.l: and the gods, all of them, were looking on.
sentences.i: and all the gods were watching them.
sentences.n: θεοὶ δ’ ἐς πάντες ὁρῶντο: ἐς … ὁρῶντο is ἐσορῶντο, ‘were looking at’, split by tmesis with πάντες put between the parts. The object, ‘them’, is not stated. The scene now moves to the gods on Olympus.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the father of men and of gods:
sentences.i: Among them the father of men and of gods was first to speak:
sentences.n: τοῖσι ‘among them’ means the gods. μύθων ἦρχε is ‘began the speeches’, ἄρχω taking the genitive, so Zeus is the first to speak. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε ‘the father of men and of gods’ is a formula for Zeus, and the line is the same as Odyssey 1.28. Here a speech follows at once.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ φίλον ἄνδρα διωκόμενον περὶ τεῖχος
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶμαι·
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly a dear man pursued around the wall
with my eyes I behold;
sentences.i: “Ah, truly, I see with my own eyes a man dear to me being chased round the wall;
sentences.n: Zeus speaks to the gods. ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of grief or surprise, ‘ah’, and ἦ is ‘truly’. ὁρῶμαι is ὁράομαι ‘I behold’, in the middle, with ὀφθαλμοῖσιν, the dative ‘with eyes’. διωκόμενον is the passive participle of διώκω ‘pursue’ and goes with φίλον ἄνδρα ‘a dear man’, Hector, not yet named.

sentences.t:
ἐμὸν δ’ ὀλοφύρεται ἦτορ
Ἕκτορος, ὅς μοι πολλὰ βοῶν ἐπὶ μηρί’ ἔκηεν
Ἴδης ἐν κορυφῇσι πολυπτύχου,
sentences.l:
and my heart grieves
for Hector, who for me many thigh-pieces of oxen burned
on the peaks of many-folded Ida,
sentences.i: and my heart grieves for Hector, who burned many thigh-pieces of oxen for me on the peaks of many-folded Ida,
sentences.n: ἐμὸν … ἦτορ ‘my heart’ is the subject of ὀλοφύρεται, ‘grieves for’, which takes the genitive Ἕκτορος. ὅς μοι … ἔκηεν is ‘who burned for me’; ἔκηεν is the epic aorist of καίω (ἔκηα), and ἐπί is a separated prefix (tmesis) to it. πολλὰ βοῶν … μηρία is ‘many thigh-pieces of oxen’, burned as a sacrifice, with βοῶν the genitive plural of βοῦς. Ἴδης is ‘of Ida’ and πολυπτύχου ‘many-folded’.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
ἐν πόλει ἀκροτάτῃ·
sentences.l:
and at other times again
in the topmost city;
sentences.i: and at other times again in the city at its very top;
sentences.n: ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε is ‘and at other times again’. ἀκροτάτῃ is the superlative of ἄκρος ‘topmost’, with the dative ἐν πόλει; it means the highest part of Troy, the high citadel.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖτέ ἑ δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἄστυ πέρι Πριάμοιο ποσὶν ταχέεσσι διώκει.
sentences.l:
but now again heavenly Achilles
around the city of Priam on swift feet pursues him.
sentences.i: but now heavenly Achilles in his turn is chasing him round the city of Priam on swift feet.
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτε is ‘but now again’, and ἑ ‘him’ is Hector, the object of διώκει ‘pursues’. ἄστυ πέρι is περὶ ἄστυ, with the preposition after its noun, ‘around the city’. ποσὶν ταχέεσσι is ‘on swift feet’ (ταχύς ‘swift’).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετε φράζεσθε θεοὶ καὶ μητιάασθε
ἠέ μιν ἐκ θανάτοιο σαώσομεν,
sentences.l:
But come, consider, gods, and take counsel
whether from death we shall save him,
sentences.i: But come, gods, think it over and take counsel whether we shall save him from death,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετε is ‘but come now’, ἄγετε being the plural imperative of ἄγω used as a call to several. φράζεσθε is the imperative of φράζομαι ‘consider’, and μητιάασθε the epic form of μητιάομαι ‘take counsel, plan’. ἠέ … ἦέ ‘whether … or’ gives the two choices; σαώσομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of σαόω ‘save’.

sentences.t:
ἦέ μιν ἤδη
Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ δαμάσσομεν ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.l:
or now to Achilles son of Peleus
shall we subdue him, good though he is.”
sentences.i: or whether we shall now let him be overcome by Achilles, son of Peleus, good man though he is.”
sentences.n: ἦέ … δαμάσσομεν is ‘or whether we shall subdue’, the aorist subjunctive of δαμάζω, with μιν ‘him’. Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ is ‘to Achilles son of Peleus’, the dative of the one to whom he would be subdued, as in ‘be subdued to others’. ἤδη is ‘now’. ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα is ‘being good’, a concession: good though he is. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Athena answers Zeus. τὸν δ’ αὖτε is ‘and him in turn’, and προσέειπε the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to’. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’ is a formula; γλαυκῶπις is the stock epithet, ‘gleaming-eyed’; its exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t: ὦ πάτερ ἀργικέραυνε κελαινεφὲς οἷον ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “O father, of the bright thunderbolt, dark-clouded, what a thing you have said!
sentences.i: “Father, of the bright thunderbolt and the dark clouds, what a thing you have said!
sentences.n: ὦ πάτερ ‘O father’ is followed by two vocative epithets of Zeus: ἀργικέραυνε ‘of the bright thunderbolt’ (ἀργής ‘bright’ + κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’) and κελαινεφές ‘dark-clouded’ (κελαινός ‘dark’ + νέφος ‘cloud’). οἷον is ‘what sort of thing’, an exclamation, and ἔειπες the aorist of εἶπον ‘say’ with an epic extra ε.

sentences.t:
ἄνδρα θνητὸν ἐόντα πάλαι πεπρωμένον αἴσῃ
ἂψ ἐθέλεις θανάτοιο δυσηχέος ἐξαναλῦσαι;
sentences.l:
A man, being mortal, long since fated by his lot,
back do you wish to loose from ill-sounding death?
sentences.i: Do you wish to loose a man, mortal as he is and long since fated by his lot, back out of ill-sounding death?
sentences.n: ἄνδρα θνητὸν ἐόντα ‘a man, being mortal’ is the object of ἐξαναλῦσαι, the aorist infinitive of ἐξαναλύω ‘loose out of’; ἐθέλεις is ‘you wish’ and ἂψ ‘back’. πεπρωμένον is the perfect passive participle ‘allotted, fated’, with αἴσῃ ‘by his lot’. θανάτοιο δυσηχέος is the genitive ‘out of ill-sounding death’ (δυσηχής ‘ill-sounding’); the Greek question mark is the semicolon. These lines are word for word those of Hera’s protest at 16.441–442.

sentences.t: ἔρδ’· ἀτὰρ οὔ τοι πάντες ἐπαινέομεν θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l: Do it; but we do not all approve, the other gods.”
sentences.i: Do it; but we other gods do not all approve.”
sentences.n: ἔρδ’ is ἔρδε, the imperative of ἔρδω ‘do’, with its vowel elided. ἀτάρ is ‘but’, and οὔ τοι is ‘not, I tell you’. ἐπαινέομεν is ‘we approve’, with θεοὶ ἄλλοι ‘the other gods’ added after it to say who. The line is Hera’s at 16.443, and here it ends Athena’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: Zeus replies. τὴν δ’ ‘and her’ is Athena. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’ is the usual epithet and name; the form νεφεληγερέτα is the epic nominative of a word in -της.

sentences.t: θάρσει Τριτογένεια φίλον τέκος·
sentences.l: “Take courage, Tritogeneia, dear child;
sentences.i: “Take courage, Tritogeneia, dear child;
sentences.n: θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. Τριτογένεια is a title of Athena whose meaning is not known: it has been taken as ‘Triton-born’, ‘born by the river or lake Triton’, and ‘third-born’, and the English leaves it as a name. φίλον τέκος is ‘dear child’, and the unit ends at the ano teleia. Zeus’s speech begins; he has said the same words once before, at 8.39.

sentences.t:
οὔ νύ τι θυμῷ
πρόφρονι μυθέομαι, ἐθέλω δέ τοι ἤπιος εἶναι·
sentences.l:
not at all, you see, with a ready-minded heart
do I speak, and I wish to be kind to you;
sentences.i: my heart is not wholly in what I say, and I wish to be kind to you;
sentences.n: Zeus tells her he did not mean it all. οὔ νύ τι is ‘not at all, you see’, and θυμῷ πρόφρονι is ‘with a ready-minded heart’, so that the whole is ‘I do not speak with my whole heart’; the English gives the sense. μυθέομαι is ‘I speak’, first person present. ἐθέλω δέ τοι ἤπιος εἶναι is ‘and I wish to be kind to you’: τοι is ‘to you’, ἤπιος ‘kind, gentle’, and εἶναι the infinitive ‘to be’.

sentences.t: ἔρξον ὅπῃ δή τοι νόος ἔπλετο, μὴ δ’ ἔτ’ ἐρώει.
sentences.l: Do it in the way your mind has come to be, and no longer hold back.”
sentences.i: Do as your mind is set, and hang back no longer.”
sentences.n: ἔρξον is the aorist imperative of ἔρδω ‘do’. ὅπῃ δή τοι νόος ἔπλετο is ‘in the way your mind has come to be’: ὅπῃ ‘in whatever way’, νόος ‘mind’, and ἔπλετο the aorist of πέλομαι ‘come to be’. μὴ δ’ ἔτ’ ἐρώει is ‘and no longer hold back’, with μηδέ printed as two words and ἐρώει the imperative of ἐρωέω ‘draw back’. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε πάρος μεμαυῖαν Ἀθήνην·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on Athena, already eager;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on Athena, who was already eager;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is an aorist participle of εἶπον. ὄτρυνε is the unaugmented imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, with the object Ἀθήνην. πάρος ‘already, before’ goes with μεμαυῖαν, the feminine perfect participle of μέμαα ‘be eager’, which agrees with Ἀθήνην.

sentences.t: βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα.
sentences.l: and she went down from the peaks of Olympus, darting.
sentences.i: and she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus.
sentences.n: βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’. κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων is ‘down from the peaks of Olympus’, with κατά and the genitive meaning ‘down from’ and καρήνων the genitive plural of κάρηνα (literally ‘heads’, here peaks). ἀΐξασα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. The part ends with Athena’s descent; what she does on arrival comes next.
